paragraphs.source_en: "It is true. My old father actually once asked the price. I must have been about six at the time, and I had gone out walking with him from Aburamachi toward Toorimachi. From the opposite direction someone came shouting in a loud voice, 'Any little girls wanted? Any little girls wanted?' When we reached the corner of Second Street, in front of a draper's shop called Isegen, we ran into the man. Isegen was one of Shizuoka's great establishments, a shop ten bays wide. Next time you go to Shizuoka, have a look at it; it is still there today, a very respectable firm. Its manager was named Jinbei, and he always sat at the accounts desk with a face as mournful as if his mother had died three days before. Beside Jinbei there was always a young clerk of twenty-four or twenty-five called Hatsu. This Hatsu, moreover, was a devotee of the priest Unsho, and he always had a gaunt, dark face, as though he had spent twenty-one days living on nothing but plain noodle broth. Next to Hatsu sat the apprentice Cho, a young fellow who looked as gloomy as if he had been burnt out of his house the day before, leaning his body against an abacus; and sitting shoulder to shoulder with Cho..."

paragraphs.source_en: Meitei said, "Not at all. This material is of great reference value for comparing the character of women in the twentieth century with that around the beginning of the Meiji era. I cannot lightly abandon it. So, as I was saying, when my old father and I came in front of Isegen, the child-seller saw him and said, 'Sir, would you care for a little girl? These are the last of the lot; I will let you have one cheaply, so please buy.' As he said this, he put down his carrying pole and wiped away his sweat. When I looked, there was one in each of the two baskets, front and back, both little girls about two years old. My old father said to the man, 'If the price is low, I might consider it.' And he asked, 'What, are these the only two left?' The man answered, 'Unfortunately, I have sold out everything today and only these two are left. Please choose whichever you like.' With that, he lifted up one of the girls in both hands and held her out under my old father's nose as though he were selling a squash. My old father tapped the girl's head several times, pop, pop, and said, 'Ah, that sound is not bad.' Then the bargaining began in earnest, and after he had beaten the price down thoroughly, my old father asked, 'I can buy her, but the quality is reliable, is it not?' The man said, 'Yes, yes, the one in front I have been watching all along, so there is no mistake there. But as for the one carried behind, since I have no eyes in the back of my head, there may possibly be some crack in her. If you want that one, I cannot guarantee the quality, but I can reduce the price a little.' I still remember that exchange vividly. Even in my childish heart at the time, I had already concluded that women were indeed creatures one could not relax one's guard against for a single moment. But in this year of Meiji thirty-eight, such barbarous behavior as hawking little girls about for sale no longer exists, and we no longer seem to hear claims that the girl in the rear basket is unsafe because the seller cannot keep an eye on her. Therefore, in my opinion, thanks after all to Western civilization, women's conduct has made considerable progress. What do you think, Kangetsu?"
